title: Retweets Britain First Anti-Muslim Videos
description_short: Trump retweeted anti-Muslim videos from the far-right British group Britain First, amplifying extremist propaganda and sparking international backlash.
description_medium: On November 29, 2017, Donald Trump retweeted three anti-Muslim videos posted by Jayda Fransen, deputy leader of the British far-right group Britain First. Their captions portrayed Muslims as perpetrators of violence. The posts drew condemnation from civil-rights groups and British officials, including Prime Minister Theresa May; the White House defended the president’s focus on border security.
description_long: On November 29, 2017, President Donald Trump retweeted three videos posted by Jayda Fransen, deputy leader of Britain First, a far-right British nationalist group. The captions presented the clips as examples of Muslims committing violence: one showed a person being pushed from a roof, another a boy with crutches being attacked, and a third a statue being damaged. Reporting by PBS and Reuters emphasized that the captions did not establish the people’s religion or the context of every clip; in one case, the footage involved a fight between teenagers and the boys’ religion was not reported. The retweets reached Trump’s large audience and prompted criticism in the United States and Britain. Prime Minister Theresa May’s spokesman called them wrong, while civil-rights groups objected to their anti-Muslim framing. White House press secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders said the president was highlighting security and border concerns, but said she was not aware that he endorsed Britain First. The episode documented the amplification of inflammatory, weakly contextualized videos by a sitting president and an international diplomatic reaction; it did not verify the captions’ claims.

preserved_fields.title: Retweets Britain First Anti-Muslim Videos
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump retweeted anti-Muslim videos from the far-right British group Britain First, amplifying extremist propaganda and sparking international backlash.

notes: PBS and Reuters report that Fransen posted the three videos and identify the reported scenes; PBS notes one clip showed teenagers fighting and their religion was not given. BBC reports that Theresa May’s office called the retweets wrong. The video captions were not treated as verified descriptions.

title: Trump Proposes Ukraine Cede 20% of Its Territory to Russia for Ceasefire
description_short: Trump Proposes Ukraine Cede 20% of Its Territory to Russia for Ceasefire
description_medium: On March 17, 2025, Reuters reported that Donald Trump said he and Vladimir Putin would discuss land and power plants in talks about ending Russia’s war on Ukraine. Trump said negotiators were already discussing “dividing up certain assets.” The reporting confirms discussion of territory, but not a plan requiring Ukraine to cede 20% of its territory.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Proposes Ukraine Cede 20% of Its Territory to Russia for Ceasefire
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Proposes Ukraine Cede 20% of Its Territory to Russia for Ceasefire

notes: Needs context: the assigned AP URL https://apnews.com/article/russia-ukraine-war-trump-plan-92b2c89b62f4326ff67abc5613c9b59e resolves to AP coverage of a later 28-point draft, not a March 15, 2025 proposal. The focused Reuters search for March 2025 confirms Trump said he would discuss land and power plants with Putin, but does not support the title/synopsis claim that he proposed Ukraine cede 20% of its territory. A March 17 AP account describes a 30-day ceasefire proposal, not that territorial percentage. The available sources do not support a complete long description of the title’s asserted event; a contemporaneous source or correction is needed.

title: Jared Kushner Uses WhatsApp for Foreign Government Communications
description_short: Jared Kushner Uses WhatsApp for Foreign Government Communications
description_medium: In March 2019, House Oversight chairman Elijah Cummings disclosed that Jared Kushner’s lawyer had told the committee Kushner used WhatsApp for official White House business, including communications with foreign contacts. Cummings said the practice raised federal-records and security concerns. Kushner’s lawyer disputed that he had confirmed contacts with foreign leaders and said Kushner followed White House protocols.
description_long: The House Oversight and Reform Committee was already examining whether senior Trump administration officials used private accounts in ways that violated federal recordkeeping rules when chairman Elijah Cummings disclosed new information in March 2019. Cummings said Jared Kushner’s attorney had told the committee that Kushner, a senior White House adviser, used the encrypted messaging service WhatsApp for official business, including with foreign contacts. Cummings argued that the disclosure heightened questions under the Presidential Records Act and about security. The lawyer, Abbe Lowell, disputed the committee’s account that he had confirmed Kushner communicated with foreign “leaders” or “officials”; he said Kushner followed White House protocols and directed questions to White House counsel. The disagreement matters: the public letter summarized a committee interview but did not provide a transcript resolving precisely what was said or identify every message or recipient. The report therefore supports an account of the official-use allegation and the oversight dispute, not a definitive finding that a particular message was lost, classified, or illegal. It formed part of a broader congressional inquiry into preservation of official communications by Trump administration staff.

preserved_fields.title: Jared Kushner Uses WhatsApp for Foreign Government Communications
preserved_fields.description_short: Jared Kushner Uses WhatsApp for Foreign Government Communications

notes: The New York Times and NPR report Cummings’s description of Kushner’s attorney’s statements and Lowell’s dispute over whether foreign leaders were specifically mentioned. The available reports do not identify particular WhatsApp messages or establish that a message was deleted or a law violated.

title: Revokes California Clean Air Waiver
description_short: EPA and NHTSA withdrew California’s waiver to set stricter vehicle emissions standards.
description_medium: On September 19, 2019, the Trump administration withdrew California’s Clean Air Act waiver for greenhouse-gas and zero-emission-vehicle standards. EPA and NHTSA said federal law preempted those state rules under the SAFE Vehicles program. California officials and environmental groups said the move would weaken emissions protections and announced plans to challenge it in court.
description_long: The Trump administration’s September 2019 action targeted California’s authority to set vehicle standards stricter than federal requirements. EPA withdrew a waiver granted in 2013 for California’s greenhouse-gas and zero-emission-vehicle programs, while the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration asserted that federal fuel-economy law preempted state and local rules of that kind. The agencies framed the action as creating a single national standard under the Safer Affordable Fuel-Efficient Vehicles program. They said the change did not affect California’s separate authority over standards addressing smog-forming emissions. California officials and environmental organizations argued that withdrawing the waiver would block stronger pollution controls and pledged to sue; the states’ ensuing challenge made the issue a prolonged federal-court dispute. The rollback also raised stakes for automakers, some of which had separately reached a voluntary emissions framework with California. The action did not itself rewrite every federal vehicle standard: it challenged the state’s ability to apply its greenhouse-gas and zero-emission requirements. This entry records the waiver withdrawal and the competing legal positions, rather than treating the administration’s preemption theory as a settled court ruling.

preserved_fields.title: Revokes California Clean Air Waiver
preserved_fields.description_short: EPA and NHTSA withdrew California’s waiver to set stricter vehicle emissions standards.

notes: The Department of Transportation’s release says EPA withdrew California’s waiver for greenhouse-gas and zero-emission programs while NHTSA asserted federal preemption; it says California’s smog-emissions program was not affected. AP reports California’s promised court challenge and critics’ pollution concerns. The preemption issue was contested.

title: Judge Finds Trump Liable for Business Fraud
description_short: A New York judge ruled that Trump committed fraud by overstating asset values in the civil case brought by the state attorney general.
description_medium: On September 26, 2023, New York Supreme Court Justice Arthur Engoron granted partial summary judgment to Attorney General Letitia James in her civil fraud case against Donald Trump and his company. He found that financial statements used to obtain loans and insurance included fraudulent asset valuations; other claims and the question of penalties remained for trial.
description_long: The September 26 ruling addressed the central liability question in New York Attorney General Letitia James’s civil lawsuit against Trump, his company and other defendants. Justice Arthur Engoron found that annual financial statements used in business dealings contained fraudulent valuations of Trump’s assets and overstated his net worth. The judge cited properties including Mar-a-Lago, Trump Tower and office buildings and golf courses. Reuters reported that the figures overstated Trump’s net worth by between $812 million and $2.2 billion, according to evidence submitted by James. The ruling came on partial summary judgment, so it resolved the state’s fraud claim without a trial on that issue; several other claims, including the state’s request for financial penalties, still awaited trial. The decision also ordered the cancellation of business certificates for some Trump entities and placed certain property companies under receivership, subject to further proceedings. Trump denied wrongdoing and said he would appeal. The ruling was a civil finding by a state judge, not a criminal conviction, and later proceedings addressed remedies and remaining claims. This distinction is important because the initial decision established liability but did not yet determine the final monetary penalty.

preserved_fields.title: Judge Finds Trump Liable for Business Fraud
preserved_fields.description_short: A New York judge ruled that Trump committed fraud by overstating asset values in the civil case brought by the state attorney general.

notes: Reuters and AP describe Engoron’s partial summary-judgment ruling, the asset-valuation findings, the remaining claims and penalties, and the distinction between civil liability and criminal guilt. The reports identify the decision as an initial ruling before the trial on remedies.
